label: A15
title: Chapter 15: Advanced Topics for the Community Medicine Researcher

blocks.html: Checkpoint 15.1

1. A colleague says, “Model B has lower AIC than model A, so model B is the true model.” What is the overstatement?

AIC ranks only the candidates actually compared. A lower AIC means B has the better fit-versus-complexity trade-off of the two, judged by −2 ln L + 2k on these data. It says nothing about whether B is correct, causally meaningful, or even a good model: both candidates could be poor, and a model not considered could be better. With a small AIC difference (as in §15.1.2, 557.16 against 558.25) the data barely prefer one over the other, and BIC may disagree.

2. Why does adding a purely random predictor never lower a model’s maximised likelihood? Give the argument, not just the conclusion.

The larger model contains the smaller one: setting the new coefficient to 0 reproduces the smaller model exactly, with the same likelihood. Maximum likelihood for the larger model searches over all values of that coefficient, including 0, so its maximum can only be equal to or higher than the smaller model’s. In a real sample the best value of the new coefficient is almost never exactly 0 (chance alignment with noise), so the likelihood rises slightly. This is why raw fit cannot choose model size and a penalty or a test is needed.

3. A logistic model on 400 children has ln L = −210.4 with 4 parameters. Adding a four-category feeding-practice variable gives ln L = −205.9. Compute the LR statistic, its df, the change in AIC and the change in BIC. Which criteria favour the larger model?

  1. LR = −2 × (−210.4 − (−205.9)) = −2 × (−4.5) = 9.0.
  2. A four-category variable adds 3 parameters, so df = 3. p = P(χ²₃ > 9.0) = 0.029.
  3. ΔAIC = (change in −2 ln L) + 2 × 3 = −9.0 + 6 = −3.0: AIC falls, so AIC favours the larger model.
  4. ΔBIC = −9.0 + 3 × ln 400 = −9.0 + 3 × 5.99 = −9.0 + 17.97 = +8.97: BIC rises, so BIC favours the smaller model.
  5. The LRT (p = 0.029) and AIC favour adding feeding practice; BIC, with its heavier penalty, does not.
Checkpoint 15.2

1. A thesis protocol says, “Variables with p < 0.2 in univariable analysis will be entered into a multivariable model, and backward elimination will give the final model of risk factors for low birthweight.” Give two problems, one about each step.

Univariable screening: a confounded risk factor can show no crude association and appear only after adjustment, so the screen can wrongly discard important variables (Sun, Shook & Kay, 1996). Backward elimination: the final model depends on the sample and the criterion, is unstable, and the p-values and CIs of the survivors ignore the selection, so they are too optimistic (Heinze et al., 2018). A better protocol states the aim. For the effect of one exposure, choose the adjustment set from a DAG; for a list of predictors, pre-specify candidates and validate the model.

2. For a model predicting which pregnant women will miss their third antenatal visit, is it acceptable to include a variable that is not a cause of missing the visit? Would the same variable be acceptable in a model estimating the effect of ASHA home visits on attendance?

In a predictive model, yes: any variable available at the time of prediction that improves accuracy in new data is acceptable, whether or not it is a cause. In an explanatory model of ASHA visits, not automatically: variables enter because the DAG shows they block backdoor paths. A variable that is a consequence of ASHA visits (a mediator) or a collider must be left out, and one unrelated to the question adds nothing.

3. In the CBHI bootstrap of §15.1.3, household size entered 15.5% of the final AIC-selected models. Out of 200 bootstrap samples, how many is that, and what does it tell you about a single stepwise run?

0.155 × 200 = 31 samples. A variable with no detectable association with membership was selected in about one run in six, so a variable’s presence in a single stepwise model is weak evidence that it matters. Reporting inclusion frequencies shows how much the “final model” depends on the particular sample.
Checkpoint 15.3

1. A survey samples 800 households from 40 villages (20 households per village) with an ICC of 0.10. Compute the DEFF, the effective sample size and the factor by which standard errors grow.

  1. DEFF = 1 + (20 − 1) × 0.10 = 1 + 1.9 = 2.9.
  2. Effective sample size = 800 ÷ 2.9 ≈ 276 households.
  3. DEFT = √2.9 = 1.70: standard errors are about 1.7 times their SRS values (not 2.9 times; DEFF acts on the variance).

2. One-way ANOVA of a 0/1 outcome across 30 anganwadi centres, 10 children each, gives MSB = 0.40 and MSW = 0.20. Estimate the ICC.

  1. σ̂²_b = (MSB − MSW) ÷ m = (0.40 − 0.20) ÷ 10 = 0.020.
  2. ICC = 0.020 ÷ (0.020 + 0.20) = 0.091.
  3. Check: (0.40 − 0.20) ÷ [0.40 + 9 × 0.20] = 0.20 ÷ 2.20 = 0.091. (The implied DEFF is 1 + 9 × 0.091 = 1.82.)

3. A colleague reports only the inflated variance from a DEFF and stops there. What is missing from the analysis of the exposure–outcome association?

DEFF describes how much precision clustering costs; it is a planning and variance concept. It does not produce an adjusted estimate of an association or a valid test of it. That needs an analysis that handles the clustering: a mixed-effects model (cluster-specific effects), GEE with cluster-robust SEs (population-averaged effects), or a design-based survey analysis with PSUs, strata and weights.
Checkpoint 15.4

1. A programme manager wants to know which villages have unusually low baseline CBHI membership so that she can target them. Would a mixed-effects model or GEE better suit this goal, and why?

A mixed-effects model. It estimates each village’s random intercept, shrunk towards the average so that small villages are not over-interpreted, and so answers “how does this village differ from the rest?”. GEE treats within-village correlation as a nuisance and estimates a population-averaged effect; it gives no village-specific estimates.

2. Explain why “fixed” and “random” effects are not statements about whether something was chosen at random.

The labels describe how the cluster-specific values are modelled. A fixed effect is estimated as its own separate parameter; a random effect treats the cluster values as draws from a shared distribution, which lets the model borrow strength across clusters. The same 20 villages could be modelled either way, however they were selected.

3. A cluster trial randomises 8 PHCs. GEE with exchangeable correlation gives a log OR of −0.40 for the intervention, with a robust SE of 0.10; the model-based SE is 0.16. Compute the 95% CI for the OR with each SE. Which SE should worry you, and what would you do?

  1. OR = exp(−0.40) = 0.67.
  2. Robust SE: exp(−0.40 ± 1.96 × 0.10) = exp(−0.596) to exp(−0.204) = 0.55 to 0.82.
  3. Model-based SE: exp(−0.40 ± 1.96 × 0.16) = exp(−0.714) to exp(−0.086) = 0.49 to 0.92.

The robust SE. With only 8 clusters the sandwich estimator is imprecise and tends to be too small, so tests based on it reject too often (Mancl & DeRouen, 2001). A robust SE smaller than the model-based one is a warning, not extra precision. Use a small-sample correction (the Mancl–DeRouen bias-corrected estimator; in their simulations the jackknife was no better than the robust SE), use t-based inference with few degrees of freedom, or analyse at the cluster level, and report the more conservative result.
Checkpoint 15.5

1. A block survey samples 100 women from each of two strata: a town of 5,000 women and rural areas with 45,000. Compute each stratum’s weight. If 30 town women and 50 rural women are anaemic, compute the unweighted and weighted prevalence.

  1. Town: π = 100/5,000 = 0.02, weight = 50. Rural: π = 100/45,000, weight = 450.
  2. Unweighted prevalence = (30 + 50) ÷ 200 = 40%.
  3. Weighted: Σwy = 50 × 30 + 450 × 50 = 1,500 + 22,500 = 24,000; Σw = 50 × 100 + 450 × 100 = 50,000. Prevalence = 24,000 ÷ 50,000 = 48%.
  4. The unweighted figure gives the over-sampled town (30% anaemic) half the influence although it holds only 10% of the women.

2. An NFHS analysis of 1,200 children in 60 PSUs across 6 strata reports a naive SE of 1.2 percentage points and a design-based SE of 1.8. What is the DEFF, and how many degrees of freedom does the design have?

DEFF = (1.8 ÷ 1.2)² = 1.5² = 2.25. Design degrees of freedom = PSUs − strata = 60 − 6 = 54 (not 1,199).

3. A student wants the prevalence of anaemia among adolescent girls and deletes all other women from the dataset before declaring the survey design. What should she do instead, and why?

Declare the design on the full dataset and then restrict it with the software’s subpopulation (domain) option (in R, subset(design, age < 20)). Deleting rows first can drop PSUs or whole strata that contain no adolescents, which changes the design’s degrees of freedom and, in some designs, the SE (and can stop the calculation when a stratum is left with one PSU). subset() keeps “the original design information about number of clusters, strata” (Lumley, survey package documentation).
Checkpoint 15.6

1. After propensity-score matching, a covariate’s p-value comparing the two groups is 0.62. A colleague concludes that balance was achieved. Why is this premature, and what should be reported instead?

A p-value depends on sample size, and matching usually shrinks the sample, so a covariate that is still clearly imbalanced can give a large p-value. Balance is a property of the sample, not a hypothesis about a population. Report the standardised mean difference for every covariate, before and after matching; a common convention treats |SMD| < 0.1 as negligible (Austin, 2009).

2. Before matching, mean age of mothers is 27.0 years (SD 4.0) among members and 25.0 years (SD 5.0) among non-members. Compute the SMD. Is the imbalance negligible by the usual convention?

SMD = (27.0 − 25.0) ÷ √[(4.0² + 5.0²)/2] = 2.0 ÷ √20.5 = 2.0 ÷ 4.53 = 0.44. Far above 0.1: a substantial imbalance.

3. A team matches 1:1 on the propensity score and reports an odds ratio from ordinary (unpaired) logistic regression on the matched sample. What must the team justify, and what are the two positions in the literature?

They must justify ignoring the pairs. Austin’s (2011b) simulations found that paired methods (for a binary outcome, McNemar’s test and the matched-pair OR b/c, or conditional logistic regression; or robust SEs clustered on the pair) gave type I error and CI coverage closer to nominal. Stuart (2010) records a debate and gives reasons why accounting for the pairs may not be necessary, since matching on the score does not create pairs that are alike on every covariate. The team should state which estimand (ATT among the matched) and which analysis it chose, and report the other as a sensitivity check.
Checkpoint 15.7

1. 15% of income values are missing, mostly among the wealthiest respondents, who are reluctant to disclose income. Will standard MAR-based multiple imputation remove the bias? What should the analyst do?

Not necessarily. If high income itself causes non-response, the data are MNAR: even within groups defined by the observed variables, the missing incomes are higher than the observed ones. Standard MI assumes MAR and would impute values that are too low. The analyst should include every variable that predicts income or its missingness (to make MAR as plausible as possible), then run a sensitivity analysis that imputes incomes shifted upwards by stated amounts and report whether the conclusion changes.

2. Five imputed datasets give estimates 2.0, 2.4, 2.2, 1.8 and 2.1 for a regression coefficient, each with SE 0.30. Apply Rubin’s rules to find the pooled estimate and its SE.

  1. Q̄ = (2.0 + 2.4 + 2.2 + 1.8 + 2.1) ÷ 5 = 10.5 ÷ 5 = 2.10.
  2. Ū = 0.30² = 0.09 (all five SEs equal).
  3. Deviations from 2.10: −0.1, 0.3, 0.1, −0.3, 0.0; squares sum to 0.20. B = 0.20 ÷ (5 − 1) = 0.05.
  4. T = 0.09 + (1 + 1/5) × 0.05 = 0.09 + 0.06 = 0.15. SE = √0.15 = 0.387, compared with 0.30 in any single completed dataset.

3. Why might the imputation model for missing income include “survey enumerator ID”, a variable that will never appear in the analysis model?

The imputation model’s job is to make MAR plausible and to predict the missing values well. Non-response often depends on who asked the question, so enumerator ID can explain the missingness; including it moves the mechanism towards MAR given the observed data. It has no role in the research question, so it stays out of the analysis model. The two models serve different purposes (Sterne et al., 2009).
Checkpoint 15.8

1. An ROC curve for a new biomarker lies almost on the diagonal. A second analyst reports an AUC of 0.21 for another marker. What does each result mean, and what should the second analyst check first?

The diagonal is where sensitivity equals the false-positive proportion (1 − specificity) at every cut-off: the test is no better than chance, AUC ≈ 0.5. An AUC of 0.21 is far from chance: the marker separates the groups well, but in the opposite direction to the one specified. The analyst should first check the direction (for example, whether low values indicate disease, as with MUAC). Reversing it gives AUC = 1 − 0.21 = 0.79.

2. A study has 8 diseased and 5 non-diseased people. Of the 40 diseased–non-diseased pairs, the diseased person has the higher biomarker value in 30, the values are tied in 4, and the non-diseased person is higher in 6. Compute the AUC.

AUC = (pairs won + ½ × ties) ÷ all pairs = (30 + ½ × 4) ÷ 40 = 32/40 = 0.80. (Check: 30 + 4 + 6 = 40 = 8 × 5.)

3. In the MUAC example, compute Youden’s J and LR+ at the cut-offs ≤ 12.3 cm and ≤ 12.9 cm. Which would you recommend for community screening, and why does J not settle the question?

≤ 12.3 cm: Se 0.7, Sp 0.9. J = 0.7 + 0.9 − 1 = 0.6; LR+ = 0.7/(1 − 0.9) = 7.0. ≤ 12.9 cm: Se 0.9, Sp 0.7. J = 0.9 + 0.7 − 1 = 0.6; LR+ = 0.9/0.3 = 3.0 (LR− = 0.1/0.7 = 0.14). J is identical, because J counts a missed case and a false alarm as equally bad. In community screening for SAM, a missed child may die while a false positive costs one referral visit, so ≤ 12.9 cm (higher sensitivity) is preferable. The choice rests on the costs of the two errors and on the referral capacity, not on J.
Checkpoint 15.9

1. Two logistic prediction models for 1-year TB treatment default both have a c-statistic of 0.78 in a validation sample. Model A’s calibration slope is 1.02 and intercept 0.01; model B’s slope is 1.0 but it predicts every patient’s risk about twice too high. What does the shared c-statistic tell you, and what does it fail to tell you? Which model would you give to a counsellor who quotes risks to patients?

The c-statistic measures discrimination: in 78% of defaulter–non-defaulter pairs, both models give the defaulter the higher predicted risk. Both rank patients equally well. It says nothing about calibration, whether the predicted probabilities are numerically right. Model B would tell a patient with a true 10% risk that the risk is about 20%. For ranking patients to target extra support, either would do; for quoting risks, use model A (slope ≈ 1 and intercept ≈ 0 mean its probabilities match observed frequencies), or recalibrate B’s intercept first.

2. A model’s apparent Somers’ Dxy is 0.60. Bootstrap validation gives an average optimism of 0.06 in Dxy and a corrected calibration slope of 0.85. Compute the apparent and corrected c-statistics, and explain what a slope of 0.85 says about the predictions.

C = 0.5 + Dxy/2. Apparent C = 0.5 + 0.60/2 = 0.80. Corrected Dxy = 0.60 − 0.06 = 0.54, so corrected C = 0.5 + 0.54/2 = 0.77. A calibration slope of 0.85 (below 1) means the predictions are too extreme: in new patients, high predicted risks will be too high and low ones too low, a sign of overfitting. The log-odds predictions should be shrunk towards the mean (for example, multiplied by 0.85) before use.

3. A team reports “Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.48, so the model is well calibrated” for 500 households. Why is this conclusion too strong? What would you expect the same test to show if the same model, with the same small miscalibration, were checked in 50,000 households?

A non-significant test is absence of evidence, not evidence of good calibration. The HL test has low power in samples of a few hundred, its result depends on the arbitrary grouping into tenths, and it gives no information about how the model is miscalibrated. A calibration plot with slope and intercept is more informative. In 50,000 households the same small miscalibration would very probably be significant: the test’s power rises with n, and in simulations with 50,000 patients a 0.4% deviation made it significant in every model (Kramer & Zimmerman, 2007). Significance there would not mean the model is useless.
Checkpoint 15.10

1. A trial was sized at 91 girls per arm for 80% power with 1:1 allocation. For recruitment reasons the investigators switch to 2:1 (intervention:control) but keep the same total of 182. Compute the relative efficiency and the new power. How many girls would 2:1 need to keep 80% power?

For k:1 allocation the variance of the difference is (1 + k)²/(4k) times that of 1:1 at the same total. For k = 2: 9/8 = 1.125, so the relative efficiency is 8/9 = 0.889 (11% information lost). At 1:1, Δ/SE = z_α/2 + z_β = 1.960 + 0.842 = 2.802. At 2:1 it falls to 2.802/√1.125 = 2.641. Power = Φ(2.641 − 1.960) = Φ(0.681) = 0.75, down from 0.80: a modest loss. To keep 80% power: 180.8 × 1.125 = 203.4 → n₁ = 67.8 → 68 and n₂ = 135.6 → 136, 204 girls in all (about 22 more).

2. A calculation gives 200 per group, but 20% loss to follow-up is expected. What should the enrolment target be, and why is 200 × 1.2 slightly wrong?

Enrol n/(1 − loss) = 200/0.80 = 250 per group, so that 80% of 250 = 200 complete the study. 200 × 1.2 = 240 would leave only 0.80 × 240 = 192, below the required 200. The calculated n assumes complete data on everyone analysed.

3. A cohort study will compare 1-year diarrhoea risk in infants of mothers with and without a latrine at home. Risk without a latrine is 15%; the smallest important difference is a fall to 10%. Compute n per group for 80% power at α = 0.05, and then allow for 10% loss to follow-up.

p₁ = 0.15, p₂ = 0.10, p̄ = 0.125, Δ = 0.05. √(2p̄q̄) = √(2 × 0.125 × 0.875) = √0.21875 = 0.4677. √(p₁q₁ + p₂q₂) = √(0.1275 + 0.0900) = √0.2175 = 0.4664. n = (1.960 × 0.4677 + 0.8416 × 0.4664)² ÷ 0.05² = (0.9167 + 0.3925)² ÷ 0.0025 = 1.7140 ÷ 0.0025 = 685.6 → 686 per group. With 10% loss: 685.6/0.90 = 761.8 → 762 per group (1,524 infants). (Software gives the same 685.6.)
Checkpoint 15.11

1. A meta-analysis of ten trials shows I² = 68%. A colleague says: “I² is over 50%, so we must use a random-effects model.” What reasoning does this shortcut, and what should come first?

The model should be chosen before the data are pooled, on clinical and methodological grounds: are the trials similar enough in population, intervention, comparator and outcome definition to share one true effect? If not, or if in doubt, a random-effects model (estimating the mean of a distribution of true effects) fits the question. I² can then confirm or challenge that judgement, but it is a descriptive proportion with conventional, overlapping bands (Higgins et al., 2003; Cochrane Handbook), not a switch. I² = 68% should also prompt a search for the sources of heterogeneity (prespecified subgroups) and a prediction interval.

2. A forest plot’s pooled diamond is narrower than every study’s CI. Explain why, using inverse-variance weights. When might a random-effects diamond be barely narrower than the most precise study?

Each study gets weight wᵢ = 1/SEᵢ², and the pooled estimate Σwᵢyᵢ/Σwᵢ has SE = 1/√Σwᵢ. Because Σwᵢ exceeds every single wᵢ, the pooled SE is smaller than every study’s SE, and the pooled CI narrower. Under a random-effects model each weight becomes 1/(SEᵢ² + τ²). When τ² is large compared with the SEᵢ², every weight is limited by τ², the pooled SE is about √(τ²/k) or more, and the diamond can be little narrower than, or even wider than, the most precise study’s CI.

3. Five studies give Q = 12.0. Compute I². Another five-study meta-analysis gives Q = 3.0: what is I², and why is it reported as that value?

df = k − 1 = 4. I² = (12.0 − 4)/12.0 = 8/12 = 66.7%. For Q = 3.0: (3.0 − 4)/3.0 = −33%, which is truncated to I² = 0%. Under H₀ (no heterogeneity), Q is expected to be about its df, and chance alone often makes it smaller. A negative excess means no evidence of heterogeneity, and a proportion of variance cannot be negative.
Checkpoint 15.12

1. A meta-analysis of six trials reports “Egger’s test p = 0.31, so there is no publication bias.” Give two reasons this conclusion is unsafe.

  1. With six studies the test has very low power; the Cochrane Handbook advises such tests only when there are at least 10 studies. A non-significant result is not evidence of absence. (ii) The test detects funnel-plot asymmetry, not publication bias as such: bias can exist without asymmetry (for example, if large as well as small null studies are unpublished), and asymmetry can arise without bias (heterogeneity, poorer quality of small studies, chance). A search of trial registries and grey literature says more about missing studies than the test does.

2. In a meta-analysis of 12 trials, the four smallest (SE of ln RR 0.50 each) report RRs of 0.40 to 0.50, and the eight largest (SE 0.10 each) cluster around 0.90. Compute the share of the total fixed-effect weight carried by the four small trials. Would a random-effects analysis increase or decrease their influence, and why does that matter here?

Weights: small trials 1/0.50² = 4 each, 16 in total; large trials 1/0.10² = 100 each, 800 in total. Share = 16/816 = 2.0%. The fixed-effect estimate is essentially that of the large trials (about 0.90). The small and large trials clearly disagree, so τ² will be positive. A random-effects model adds τ² to every variance, making the weights more equal and increasing the small trials’ influence, pulling the pooled RR towards 0.4–0.5. Here the disagreement follows study size (a small-study effect, possibly publication bias), so the random-effects estimate would be the more misleading one. Report both and discuss why the small trials differ.

3. Trim-and-fill imputes four “missing” trials and moves the pooled RR from 0.70 to 0.82. A colleague writes “the true effect is RR 0.82”. How would you rewrite the sentence?

“The pooled RR was 0.70 (with its CI). The funnel plot was asymmetric; in a sensitivity analysis assuming the asymmetry reflects unpublished studies, trim-and-fill imputed four trials and gave an RR of 0.82 (with its CI). The effect may therefore be overestimated.” Trim-and-fill assumes that the asymmetry is caused by publication bias and that the imputed studies mirror the observed ones; its estimate is a sensitivity analysis (Peters et al., 2007), not the true effect.
Checkpoint 15.13

1. With the prior Beta(20, 30), a survey in a second PHC finds 12 of 40 pregnant women anaemic. Give the posterior distribution and its mean. Is the posterior mean closer to the prior mean or to the sample proportion, and why?

Posterior = Beta(20 + 12, 30 + 28) = Beta(32, 58). Mean = 32/90 = 0.356 (95% credible interval 0.261 to 0.457 from software; by hand, SD = √[32 × 58 ÷ (90² × 91)] = 0.050, and 0.356 ± 1.96 × 0.050 = 0.257 to 0.454). Prior mean 0.40; sample proportion 12/40 = 0.30. The posterior mean is a weighted average with weights 50 (the prior’s “sample size”, a + b) and 40 (the data): (50 × 0.40 + 40 × 0.30)/90 = 0.356. It lies slightly closer to the prior (0.044 away) than to the data (0.056 away), because the prior carries more information (50) than the new sample (40).

2. A report says: “The 95% credible interval for the risk difference was 1% to 9%, so there is a 95% probability that the true risk difference lies in this range.” What condition must be added for the sentence to be correct? Could the same sentence be written about a 95% confidence interval?

It must be conditional on the prior and the model: “given the prior distribution and the statistical model used, there is a 95% posterior probability …”. With a different prior, or a wrong model, the interval and the probability change. The sentence cannot be written about a frequentist 95% CI: there the 95% refers to the method (95% of intervals built this way, over repeated samples, contain the true value), and the parameter is not given a probability distribution.

3. A clinician’s pre-test probability of tuberculous lymphadenitis is 10%. A test with LR+ 6 is positive. Compute the post-test probability, and name the prior, the likelihood and the posterior in this calculation.

Pre-test odds = 0.10/0.90 = 0.111. Post-test odds = 0.111 × 6 = 0.667. Post-test probability = 0.667/1.667 = 0.40. Prior: the pre-test probability (10%, or odds 0.111). Likelihood: the likelihood ratio, P(positive | disease)/P(positive | no disease) = 6, which carries the evidence of the result. Posterior: the post-test probability, 40%.
Checkpoint 15.14

1. A trial’s Table 1 reports baseline weight with “p = 0.04” and the authors write that “randomisation failed”. Explain why the p-value is the wrong tool and what the authors should do about a prognostically important imbalance.

If allocation was truly random and concealed, every baseline difference arose by chance, so the null hypothesis of the test is known to be true, and about 1 in 20 such tests will give p < 0.05 anyway (more when many variables are tested). A small p says nothing about whether randomisation failed; failure is judged from the process (sequence generation, concealment). What matters is whether an imbalance is large enough to affect the outcome, which depends on how prognostic the variable is, not on its p-value. The remedy is to adjust for prognostic baseline variables specified in the protocol (for example, by ANCOVA), whatever their balance, and to report baseline characteristics descriptively (Senn, 1994; Schulz & Grimes, 2002).

2. In a planned trial of a salt-reduction intervention, the correlation between baseline and 6-month systolic BP is expected to be 0.6. A final-value analysis would need 200 participants per arm. Compute the variance factors for a change-score analysis and for ANCOVA, and the corresponding sample sizes per arm.

Relative to the final-value analysis (factor 1): change score: 2(1 − ρ) = 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 → 200 × 0.8 = 160 per arm; ANCOVA: 1 − ρ² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64 → 200 × 0.64 = 128 per arm. ANCOVA needs 36% fewer participants than a final-value analysis and 20% fewer than a change-score analysis.

3. A non-inferiority trial of a community-based versus facility-based treatment for a childhood infection uses a margin of −10 percentage points. The ITT difference in cure is −3 points (95% CI −8.5 to +2.5); the per-protocol difference is −6 points (95% CI −11.8 to −0.2). What do you conclude, and why are both analyses reported?

ITT: the lower limit −8.5 lies above −10, so non-inferiority is shown. Per-protocol: the lower limit −11.8 lies below −10, so non-inferiority is not shown; the CI also lies wholly below 0, so community treatment was significantly worse among those who followed the protocol. The conclusion is that non-inferiority is not established. In a non-inferiority trial, ITT is not conservative: non-adherence and dropout in both arms make the arms look alike and bias the result towards non-inferiority (ICH, 1998). The per-protocol analysis loses the protection of randomisation, so its bias has no predictable direction; each covers the other’s weakness, so both are reported and a convincing claim needs both to agree.
